articles.title: Wiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with Canada
articles.text:
Using the bathroom or having a cry is about to become more expensive for North Americans as the US and Canada enter a full-fledged trade war that threatens to flush away decades of peaceful trading between the two nations.

After trade negotiations broke down between the two countries last weekend, Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, vowed to match US tariffs “dollar for dollar” and unveiled a list of nearly 900 American goods that will face 25% to 50% tariffs starting on 8 September.

Paper products are among the hardest-hit sectors, with Canada threatening to put tariffs of between 25% and 50% on “toilet paper or face tissue stock” from 8 September in retaliation for a 50% hike from Washington DC.

Though American toilet paper and tissues are often made domestically, they heavily rely on lumber-rich Canada for raw materials. Procter & Gamble, the owner of Charmin toilet paper, said last year that it would have to increase prices amid tariffs that were in place at the time.

The US imported $328m worth of toilet paper from Canada in 2024, according to the World Bank, making it by far the largest exporter of the product to the US. Retailers including Costco source much of their paper products from the country.

The US accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption despite having only 4% of the world’s population. The average American uses 141 rolls of toilet paper per year, making them No 1 for No 2s globally, just ahead of Germans, each using an average of 134 rolls annually.

It’s not just paper products that could rise in price. The trade war highlights the deep economic ties shared between the two countries as consumers continue to worry about inflation on both sides of the border.

US tariffs are specifically affecting Canadian liquor, including popular whiskey brands Crown Royal and Canadian Club, which are currently under a 50% tariff.

While Canada has not introduced a tariff on American liquor, most Canadian provinces have introduced their own bans on American alcohol, in retaliation for earlier tariffs on Canadian products. Donald Trump used these province-wide bans on American alcohol as part of his legal justification for his new tariffs against Canada.

Carney has asked province leaders to consider putting American liquor back on the shelves, though as the Nova Scotia premier Tim Houston told CBC News: “Whether Nova Scotians or Canadians will actually buy it when it’s back on the shelves, that’s a whole other discussion.”

Trump also said that his new tariffs are in retaliation for Canadian levies against the American dairy industry. He introduced a 50% tariff on nearly all Canadian dairy products, with the exception of Canadian cheese.

In response, Canada has a 50% tariff on American dairy products, along with a 25% tariff on American cheese.

Canada also took a swing at the US fishing industry, with a 25% tariff on American fish and seafood, including frozen lobster. The move prompted Republican senator Susan Collins, facing a tough re-election battle in lobster-capital Maine, to call Trump’s latest move “a mistake”.

A 25% tariff on Canadian cars and auto parts is set to affect the American auto industry, which relies heavily on Canadian parts for manufacturing. Trump has threatened to double the tariff to 50% if a deal isn’t made by 1 January 2027.

With negotiations down the drain, it’s unclear if or when the tariffs will be lifted. But the Trump administration is adamant that “there’s no possible way” the trade dispute with Canada will affect US consumers, according to Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative.

“The fundamentals are good,” he said. “I don’t think this is going to affect anything.”

articles.title: Bill Gates calls for ‘human-reserved’ jobs in face of AI takeover
articles.text:
Bill Gates has called for “human-reserved” jobs in certain sectors to prevent AI replacing them, and expressed concern that governments are not prepared for the impact the technology will have.

In a 6,000 word essay titled The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make are critical, the billionaire Microsoft co-founder likened the need to spare roles from digital encroachment to how nature reserves operate to protect the environment.

“Many jobs will disappear forever,” he said, in his first lengthy piece on AI in three years. “I believe that as AI and robots improve, we’ll set aside certain things for only people to do.

“I’ve started calling this domain human reserved. I like the phrase human reserved because it makes me think of nature reserves – places where we could put buildings and roads, but we choose not to because the loss would be too great.”

He cited examples including the health professionals who cared for his father, who died of Alzheimer’s disease six years ago.

“Something in the care they gave my dad was irreplaceably human, no robot could or should have done it,” he said. “Imagine a robot giving you the awful news that you have an incurable disease. There’s no technical reason why it couldn’t. Yet it shouldn’t.”

Wednesday’s essay is one of Gates’s first major public interventions since he became embroiled in the Jeffrey Epstein scandal. An external review commissioned by the Gates Foundation found last month that there had been about 30 meetings between Epstein and foundation leaders and staff – including Gates – between 2011 and 2014.

Gates, who has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s crimes, remains the chair of his $89bn (£65bn) charitable foundation and previously said he regretted “every minute” he spent with the sex offender.

Gates warns in his essay that governments are not prepared for the scale of the impact of AI.

“The highest priority is a monumental task: creating a domestic and international framework for dealing with AI,” he wrote. “After the attacks of 9/11 the US government went through its biggest reorganisation since World War II for the purpose of improving just one function, national security.

“AI will require much, much more. It will affect national security as well as employment, education, taxation, energy, elections, air and water, public health, the financial system, law enforcement, transportation, public lands and IT systems.

“It is fair to wonder whether the world’s institutions are up to the task of designing and implementing this new architecture.”

Gates also said that as part of a global effort “some cooperation between the US and China will be required”.

His staff are working to set up a meeting with China’s president, Xi Jinping, in November to discuss global efforts to mitigate the growing risks posed by AI.

Gates last met Xi three years ago, when he became the first foreign entrepreneur the Chinese president had hosted since the global Covid pandemic.

The tech billionaire also expressed concern in his essay about the impact of AI on education.

articles.title: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on wide range of US goods
articles.text:
Canada has announced it will impose tariffs on a wide range of key American industries including cosmetics, dairy, wood products and outdoor equipment in the coming weeks, as it retaliates roughly “dollar for dollar” against levies imposed by the US.

In a strong Canadian countermove to tariffs levied by Donald Trump, which took effect on Saturday after trade talks collapsed the day before, Canada’s finance and industry ministers on Tuesday called the measure a “focused response” to what they see as unfair trade practices.

The White House claimed it was using section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to protest against “discriminatory” trade policies by Canada, including provincial bans on US alcohol – a ban that was only implemented in protest against tariffs imposed on Canadian goods last year.

The prime minister, Mark Carney, had previously pledged a “dollar-for-dollar” response from his government after roughly 5% of exports to the US were singled out by the White House.

The retaliatory Canadian measures will cover C$27.6bn ($19.9bn) in imports and are meant to target key industries including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper.

The list from Ottawa has more than 700 items, ranging from from hockey sticks to ornamental fish and toilet paper to smoked lobster, with most of the tariffs set at 25% or 50%. A small group of items, including air conditioning units and tool parts, will face a lower 15% tariff. The levies will be effective starting 8 September and only apply to goods originating from the US.

In announcing the retaliatory measures, the finance minister, François-Philippe Champagne, said the country was united in its fight against the US, telling attenders that Canada remained “masters of our own home”.

The industry minister, Mélanie Joly, called on businesses and consumers to buy Canadian goods as part of a broader “resistance” movement in the trade war.

“You have power,” she said.

The government also announced more than C$7bn in support for businesses affected by the latest tariffs, adding to more than C$20bn in support announced over the past 18 months.

Canada’s decision to retaliate means both countries have doubled down on a trade war that could cost billions.

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump said he was giving “serious consideration” to changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” – reminiscent of his decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Others pointed out that Ontario, Canada’s most populous province, was named after the lake, not the other way around.

Trump’s frustration with Ontario in particular stems from his feud with the province’s premier, Doug Ford, who called the president a “loser” and the “king of bankruptcies” and told the US president to “kiss my ass”. He also threatened to cut electricity and rare earth metal exports to the US.

Trump called Ford a “flunky” of “Governor Carney” and warned “these clowns to ‘fall in line’ or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!”

Trump later alluded to revelations that his trade negotiators had looked to weaken French language rules, saying he would “never interfere” with Canadians speaking French, calling it a “lie … made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support”.

Trump later added: “I love French Canadians!”

articles.title: US Treasury’s Scott Bessent ‘will lose’ battle with bond markets, former mentor warns
articles.text:
Scott Bessent’s attempt to calm the bond markets and push down America’s cost of borrowing have attracted a rebuke from the US Treasury secretary’s former mentor.

The billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller, who worked with Bessent at George Soros’s fund management firm in the 1990s, has warned that his former pupil is courting danger by trying to suppress US bond yields.

Druckenmiller, writing in the Wall Street Journal, argued that the US should “let the bond market speak”, rather than expand its bond purchases in an effort to push up prices, and lower borrowing costs.

“Governments defending prices against fundamentals always lose. The only variable is how much they spend before conceding,” he wrote.

Druckenmiller argued that Washington should heed the rise in borrowing costs – measured by bond yields – and take steps to cut the budget deficit, rather than interfering in the market to push yields down again.

“The long-term Treasury yield is the most important price in the world. It is also the only fiscal disciplinarian the US has left. Neither party will run on entitlement reform. Both have spent the past decade expanding commitments while ignoring arithmetic,” he wrote.

Druckenmiller’s intervention comes after Bessent decided to at least double the maximum size of the Treasury’s buyback operations, from $2bn (£1.5bn) to $4bn. That move briefly led to a drop in US long-term bond yields, but this quickly reversed.

“The market’s verdict was swift and correct: This wasn’t liquidity management, it was price management – and a mistake far larger than $4bn suggests,” Druckenmiller said.

Bond yields fall when prices rise, and vice versa.

Yesterday, CNBC reported that Bessent could increase his bond-buying firepower by conducting purchases using the Treasury’s near-$1tn General Account, a government fund held at the Federal Reserve.

Last week the US national debt hit $40tn, and rising, and the annual deficit is expected to hit $2tn this year.

Addressing this primary deficit is the “only thing that durably lowers long-term yields”, Druckenmiller wrote in the WSJ.

“The reward is enormous: A credible fiscal package would do more for the long end of the curve than a buyback program 1,000 times this size,” he said.

Bessent’s bond market intervention is a signal that “Washington is increasingly uncomfortable with soaring long-term borrowing costs,” said Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG.

Bessent’s attempts to battle the financial markets are ironic, as he worked alongside Soros when he beat the Bank of England and forced the pound to crash out of the European exchange rate mechanism in 1992.

That drama, which became known as Black Wednesday, showed how hard it is for a government to defend a currency when investors believe it is overvalued.

But despite that experience, Bessent took part in a joint operation with Japan to prop up the yen earlier this month – seemingly to prevent Tokyo selling US bonds to fund yen purchases.

“The irony of the guy working for Soros and Druckenmiller who broke the Bank of England back in 1992 pretending that you can do FX intervention alone, and lastingly defend a currency, is just amazing,” Adam Posen, the president of the Peterson Institute and an expert on the Japanese economy, told the Financial Times earlier this month.

Rising geopolitical tensions have pushed bond yields higher, as the failure of the US-Iran peace talks lifted the oil price – which threatens to drive inflation higher.

The collapse of US-Canada trade talks last weekend has also put foreign policy back in the spotlight, weakening the Canadian dollar. A North American trade war could hurt US growth, creating more fiscal pressure.

articles.title: New York business group sues Mamdani over city-owned grocery stores plan
articles.text:
A New York City business group sued mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday over his plan to create five municipally owned grocery stores.

The Multicultural Business Coalition, which says it represents hundreds of small supermarkets, filed two lawsuits in New York county supreme court on Monday, arguing that the plan violates the civil rights of smaller, immigrant- and minority-owned businesses. The group argues that smaller stores would be unable to match the discounts offered by the city grocery stores and “therefore, will be put out of business,” according to the lawsuits.

During his campaign, which focused heavily on the issue of affordability, Mamdani proposed introducing city-owned, subsidized grocery stores, which he said would help combat rising food costs.

The city plans to open five stores by 2029, with one in each borough. Mamdani has said that plans call for the stores to offer some produce, meat and seafood pantry staples, dairy and other refrigerated goods at prices 30% below typical retail prices – and he has said that the program is projected to cut New Yorkers’ “average grocery bill by 15%”.

The first store is scheduled to open in the Bronx in 2027.

The first lawsuit filed on Monday against Mamdani’s plan argues that the city did not conduct any “serious analysis” of how the new stores could affect smaller neighborhood grocers before launching the initiative. The second, meanwhile, argues that the city does not have the legal authority to create the stores.

Speaking to CNN on Monday, attorney Mark Jaffe, general counsel for the Multicultural Business Coalition and president of the Greater New York Chamber of Commerce, said: “You cannot expect hard-working small business owners to compete with a supermarket that isn’t going to pay rent, won’t have to pay an electric bill and won’t have to buy their products at full price.”

He added: “They cannot possibly compete because no one will be subsidizing them.”

Mamdani defended the plan at a news conference on Monday, where he was asked about the lawsuits.

“I continue to be fully confident in both the legality and the importance of our initiative to deliver five city-run grocery stores, one in each borough, to the people of our city,” he said. “We are talking about a reflection of a cost of living crisis that has seen grocery prices increase by about 30% over the last few years, and we’re also talking about delivering five city-run grocery stores in a city of 8.5 million people that has more than a thousand grocery stores.”

He also said the city has subsidized groceries on Essex Street in Manhattan and Moore Street in Brooklyn. And he argued that they have “not had a negative effect on bodegas around them or on grocery stores around them”.

New York City’s Economic Development Corporation (EDC), which is overseeing the stores, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuits on Tuesday.

But, a spokesperson for the EDC told the New York Times on Monday that the city was “evaluating programs and policies to support local grocers”.

“We are looking at the potential for tax abatement, incentives and zoning benefits through existing city programs to ensure that the city is doing everything in our power to alleviate cost pressures for small businesses across the city,” the spokesperson added.

articles.title: Trump announces new 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and steel
articles.text:
Donald Trump announced a new 50% tariff on automobiles and crucial raw materials from Canada, the latest deterioration in trade relations between the two neighbors with historically strong economic ties.

The US president said that the increased tariffs would start on 1 January 2027 on all cars, trucks, automobile parts and steel. He also derided the nation’s tariffs on American farmers, writing on social media that Canada has been “ripping off” the US “for years”.

“On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with,” he wrote on Truth Social. “They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US! They do 95% of their business with the U.S., with us, the exact opposite!”

In response, Mark Carney told reporters on Monday that Trump’s announcement was largely expected.

“It’s not a surprise for us that the US would take some form of reprisal to our response to their unjustified tariff, which was on top of other unjustified tariffs,” the Canadian prime minister said from Quebec.

“But what message does that send to the workers in Michigan, in Ohio, in Kentucky, in Alabama, who rely on Canadian demand?” Carney continued. “We’re their largest customer for automobiles, more than the European Union, Japan, Korea, many others combined, and the United Kingdom.”

He added that Canada would be ready to move forward with talks “when the Americans go to the negotiating table first with the right attitude toward our industry and a true partnership”.

Trump’s announcement follows the last-minute collapse this weekend of a potential deal to lower tariffs on automobiles and other materials. After Trump imposed another 50% tariff on $20bn worth of Canadian exports, including hockey equipment and electronics, Carney, rejected the latest deal between the two nations on Saturday.

Carney said that the US “asked too much and they offered too little”, and he has vowed to match the American tariffs “dollar for dollar”.

articles.title: Sports Direct's Ashley attacks Burnham over 'populist' High Street revival plans
articles.text:
Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley has criticised Prime Minister Andy Burnham's cost of living and retail policies as "populist".

In a letter to Burnham, Ashley accused him of "jumping on 'everyday fixes' or bandwagons" while businesses struggled with the government's "disastrous" business rates policies and higher employment costs.

He also described a proposal to increase business rates on large warehouses in order to help reduce rates for pubs and clubs as "delusional".

A Downing Street spokesperson said Burnham would "build a new economy that backs British business, delivers growth in every postcode and ensures the essentials in life... are affordable again"

Removing the VAT from household electricity bills and reducing business rates for some firms was "just the start", the government spokesperson added.

Burnham has promised to revitalise Britain's "hollowed out" High Streets and to address cost of living concerns by tackling "rip-off Britain" including misleading discounting in shops.

Ashley's Frasers Group was built on buying up struggling brands and undercutting rivals on price. It is still owned by Ashley but now run by his son-in-law Michael Murray.

The business currently owns Sports Direct, Flannels, House of Fraser, Game, Evans Cycles, Slazenger, Jack Wills, and Gieves & Hawkes, and several other retail brands.

Ashley's letter, seen by the BBC and first reported by the Financial Times,, external hits out at the government's strategy.

"Shortsighted or populist reactions to underlying business challenges are not the answer. You have the chance to make a difference or get it horribly wrong," he wrote.

He called on Burnham to use his first Budget, scheduled for 28 October, to lower costs for employers and address business rates.

The government has launched a review of the tax on commercial properties, but in advance of that has already announced that pubs, social clubs and live music venues will get a 20% business rates cut from April.

"If your answer is to tax larger retailers even more, through hiking business rates on retailer-owned or third-party warehouses whilst reducing rates for pubs and clubs, then that is simply delusional," Ashley's letter said.

Burnham previously said before he was prime minister that cuts for pubs, clubs and music venues could be paid for by higher levies on warehouses operated by online firms such as Amazon, and targeting the owners of empty High Street properties.

Ashley built Frasers Group from a single Sports Direct store in Maidenhead in 1982 to a sprawling empire of dozens of brands employing 30,000 people.

The billionaire has frequently attracted controversy from investors and the media with accusations over the years of building success by exploiting workers.

In 2016, Ashley admitted to MPs that workers at his Derbyshire warehouse had been paid below the minimum wage and a policy of fining staff for being late was unacceptable.

The business this month bought luxury department store Harvey Nichols and promised a "significant restructuring" of the business.

In his letter to Burnham he asks: "My challenge to you is – how are you going to help with turning Harvey Nichols around?"

He also raises the issue of retail theft which he said cost Frasers Group approximately £40m a year.

Frasers Group has also been increasing its stake in menswear retailer Hugo Boss after its initial takeover bid for the German company was rejected.

articles.title: Bayern Munich season preview: What is the aim for Kompany, Kane and Bundesliga champions?
articles.text:
Bayern Munich start their latest title defence as overwhelming odds-on favourites to win the Bundesliga again - so what would consistute success this season?

The German side are as short as 1-7 odds with bookmakers after winning 13 of the past 14 titles - and are chasing a hat-trick of successes.

They host Stuttgart on Friday (19:30 BST) in a game you can watch live on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website.

Vincent Kompany's side already have a win against rivals Borussia Dortmund under their belt after winning the German Super Cup 2-1 last weekend.

England captain Harry Kane will be looking to win his fourth Bundesliga Golden Boot in four seasons... and perhaps even more.

"The targets at Bayern are always set as high as possible, which means winning the Bundesliga, winning the cup, winning the Champions League and perhaps even winning every single match," said Kompany this summer.

BBC Sport has a look at what Bayern and Kane can hope for this season - and what is new.

Winning the Bundesliga title is more of an expectation than a cause for huge celebration at the Allianz Arena.

Since 2012 only once have they not been champions - when Bayer Leverkusen went unbeaten all season domestically in 2023-24.

In Kompany's two seasons at Bayern, since leaving Burnley, they have finished 13 and 16 points clear at the top.

Last season the German double winners were one of Europe's biggest entertainers, scoring 184 goals in all competitions.

They scored a record 122 goals in the Bundesliga and 43 in the Champions League, where they fell to Paris St-Germain 6-5 on aggregate in the semi-finals.

Since this era of dominance started with the 2012-13 Treble, including the Champions League, they have only won Europe's top trophy once since then - in 2020.

But German football writer Constantin Eckner says Kompany does "not necessarily" need to win it this season.

"Bayern's hierarchy have been very happy with him and the progress of the team," said Eckner.

"As long as they compete among the top four in Europe, they are content to have Kompany. He has brought back a notion of stability to Bayern's managerial post.

"Before that, it was quite the revolving door policy, as they had seven managers in eight years.

"The Belgian has been a revelation, and the feeling is he could become one of the best managers in the world.

"One could argue he is already among the best, though games like the one at Paris St-Germain have shown that he still has a few things to learn."

When Kane joined Bayern on a four-year deal in 2022 from Tottenham there was a feeling, certainly in England, that he might return home at the end of that deal.

Kane had never won a trophy during his time at Tottenham, or with England, so the pull of going to a team who win trophies nearly every year was strong.

But many also thought after bagging a few medals he would perhaps try to break the Premier League goalscoring record (sitting 47 behind Alan Shearer).

In fact he admitted as much last week, saying: "When I first left, for sure it was something I thought - I would definitely be coming back. That itch isn't there as much anymore."

The 33-year-old has loved his time at Bayern and says he is ready to begin discussions over extending that deal.

That love is very much mutual. Bayern honorary president Uli Hoeness has called Kane "the best signing we've ever made".

This is a club who have had some legendary goalscorers in Gerd Muller, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge and Robert Lewandowski.

Kane scored 61 goals in 51 club matches last season, the most a Bayern player has ever struck in one campaign.

That took his total to 146 goals - plus 33 assists - in 147 games for Bayern. He won the European Shoe in 2024 and 2026 and 'just' the regular Bundesliga Golden Boot in 2025.

He also scored all three goals in the German Cup final win over Stuttgart to complete the 2026 double.

"There are many fans who believe he could win the Ballon d'Or," said Eckner.

"Bayern are lobbying for it [and it is] also a sign towards the much younger Michael Olise that a move to Real Madrid wouldn't be necessary to win the Ballon d'Or.

"Kane has impressed with his very consistent and relentless goalscoring in the Bundesliga. He has essentially filled the shoes of Robert Lewandowksi, who put up similar numbers.

"Bayern rely heavily on Kane. They haven't signed a real back-up for him, nor a potential replacement. His contract runs out at the end of the season, but Bayern are sure he will extend for a few more years."

Were Kane to win the Ballon d'Or he would be only the second Englishman to win it since the 1970s and the first since Michael Owen in 2001.

"The Ballon d'Or is as big as it gets, from an individual point of view," he said.

"It's not in my hands. I've done what I can do in terms of putting in the performances. It's now down to votes and other people and the media - stuff I can't control - so we'll see what happens."

However last November Kane admitted: "I could score 100 goals this season, but if I don't win the Champions League or the World Cup, you're probably not going to win the Ballon d'Or."

He lost in the semi-final of both competitions.

Another one of Bayern's irreplaceable players is another Londoner in Olise, who represents France at international level.

The forward has scored 43 goals - including one in this season's Super Cup - with 46 assists in just over two years at the club.

Bayern have made little changes rather than a squad overhaul this summer, not surprising after two good seasons.

They have recruited Germany left-back Nathaniel Brown from Eintracht Frankfurt for a fee thought to be about £47m.

The 23-year-old can also play on the wing - and even featured in the number 10 role in the Super Cup, where he scored on his debut.

The other big signing is Morocco international Ismael Saibari from PSV for a reported £43m.

Like Brown, the 27-year-old is versatile and can play in midfield or anywhere up front. He scored three times at the World Cup.

The highest profile exits have been Germany midfielder Leon Goretzka, 31, and versatile Portuguese wideman Raphael Guerreiro, 32.

Both have left as free agents at the end of their contracts.

Senegal striker Nicolas Jackson returned to Chelsea at the end of his season-long loan.

Bayern will also have to manage the situation with Jamal Musiala this season.

The 23-year-old attacking midfielder says he is being treated for a "neurological dysfunction" after collapsing during two friendlies this summer.

He added they were "temporary, brief, but easily treatable absence seizures".

"I'm receiving excellent medical treatment and am very optimistic," he continued.

"FC Bayern and my family and friends are always by my side and supporting me on this journey."

articles.title: Have expensively-assembled Rangers improved at all under McInnes?
articles.text:
Where do you start? How do you catalogue the insipidness of Derek McInnes' Rangers team in Jablonec?

How do you catalogue the Pedro-Caixinha-in-the-bushes level embarrassment that the club experienced in their exit from European football on Thursday?

In Jablonec, Rangers were unspeakably awful, devoid of any cohesion, desire, threat, their manager reduced to saying how embarrassed and mortified he was multiple times post-match.

They had one shot on target the whole night, one goal scored in 210 minutes. They lost 1-0 and then perished on penalties.

Rangers fans in the stadium gave it to them with both barrels at the end.

McInnes apologised. The whole scene was cringe-making. He tried to explain what he was trying to do with his multiple switches of formation and attempted to explain why his side were "miles off it".

Talk is cheap in his position. There's a limited shelf life for that kind of thing at Ibrox.

The chat from some Rangers folk in the preamble was that the Conference League meant little to them, that an exit wouldn't spark an uprising, that no midweek European football could give them a chance to hurl themselves at the Premiership instead. Fine in theory, but not in reality.

The notion that a defeat would be met with a collective shrug by Rangers fans was never a serious proposition. This defeat sparked untrammelled fury.

McInnes would be as well staying away from social media. Winning in the bear pit of Pittodrie on Sunday is strongly advised.

Rangers were so flat in the Czech Republic, meandering about like confused men, showing weakness in the tackle and not a scintilla of wit. McInnes changed the shape of his four or five times and the poverty of their play didn't improve one iota.

"I look at us now and I'm thinking, well, we're no' great as a possession-based team at the minute," said McInnes in explaining his constant switches.

"We're not a counter-attacking team enough, or effectively enough, at times. We don't look like a team who are happy when we go direct. And teams need to be something."

Quite. And what are Rangers? What's their identity? What are they good at? In what areas are they improving?

McInnes was appointed in June, had a full pre-season, had six games and then a week off to prepare for the trip to Jablonec, only for Rangers to produce their worst effort of this, and many other, seasons.

During the dog days of his reign at Rangers, Russell Martin was once asked if he could name one or two things that were better on his watch - and he couldn't do it.

If McInnes was asked the same question now then there's no guarantee that he would come up with an answer, or at least, an answer that rang true.

Nobody really knows what his Rangers are, least of all McInnes, you suspect. He made three substitutions at the break on Thursday, a trio that brought his total of half-time replacements to 11 in seven games.

That betrays a manager who has either got his team wrong in the first place, hasn't been able to impart his message to his starters or doesn't have a dressing room capable of taking in what he's saying to them. Whatever the truth of it, it's not good.

He knows what he wants because he watched it on television the night before. Hearts had four new players in their starting line-up against Rapid Vienna and used another two off the bench.

Wouter Vrancken, in quick time, moulded them together and made something terrific out of them in winning their own Conference League tie in Austria.

McInnes praised his old club for the resilience of their players and the stomach they showed for the fight. The inference being that his own boys had little or none of that. Again you ask, why not?

Vast periods of this play-off went by without Rangers stringing more than four and five passes together. They pressed in ones and two or not at all.

They came across as a team that had just met, a collection of guys rounded up in a pub and coached by a character who had no idea what to do with them.

What has McInnes been doing with his expensively-assembled team. A dozen players have now been signed. How much money has to be spent before the manager starts to look convincing in the role?

The Rangers players who were on the field in the Czech Republic cost about £30m in transfer fees. The wage bill at Ibrox must be astronomical. They've now added the £8.5m winger Kim Min-su and may soon recruit a £9.5m striker in Kevin Kelsy.

The giant wad of cash splurged on all this would choke an elephant.

By contrast, Jablonec's record signing cost around £700,000. Their most recent turnover was £8.5m compared to Rangers' £94m. Their stadium is the size of a shoebox, their support tiny, their European story minimal.

They were the ones who went after the game, though. They didn't have a huge amount going for them in ability terms, but they had edge and character.

Hard work and energy? They trounced Rangers on all of the things that require no talent, just honesty.

McInnes is in a tight spot, not in any danger of losing his job, but with huge amounts of ground to make up with the fans.

He's been around a long time, but the pressure those supporters can exert when things are bad is a challenge for any manager, no matter how long he's been around.

Pittodrie next. A welcome, of sorts, awaits.

articles.title: Callaway ditches golf brand Good Good over sexist video backlash
articles.text:
Golf club manufacturer Callaway has ended its partnership with content creator Good Good with immediate effect following backlash over a video which showed a woman being pushed to the ground after reaching for a club.

American golf brand Good Good has one of the most popular sport YouTube channels with 2.13m subscribers and had created and published the advert for Callaway last week.

But the video drew widespread criticism and was accused of making light of violence against women, and both companies removed the advert and issued apologies.

Good Good, who Callaway has worked with since 2023, has also stepped away from its sponsorship of a PGA Tour event in Austin, Texas in November.

On Thursday, Callaway, in a statement on X,, external conceded its content review process "was not comprehensive enough", adding that it had "listened and reflected deeply on the hurt and disappointment caused by the video we reposted".

The manufacturer said it was also donating $1m (£735,725) to organisations working to prevent violence against women and support victims.

"We heard from individuals who shared personal experiences related to violence against women, and their stories were powerful reminders that this issue touches the lives of far too many people," Callaway's statement read.

"Unequivocally, violence against women is unacceptable and should never be trivialised, normalised, or used as entertainment."

Callaway said they have taken "appropriate internal corrective actions" to help ensure this does not happen again.

The advert showed Good Good co-founder Garrett Clark rushing over to Alexis Miestowski - a professional golfer and regular content creator for Good Good - and pushing her to the ground before shouting: "Do not touch my new driver."

The brand, which has become one of the largest content creators in golf, launched its YouTube channel 2020.

Regular clips include men and women competing in various golf challenges, while Good Good also creates made-for-TV shows as well as adverts for golf clothing and other merchandise.

After pulling out as sponsors of the PGA Tour tournament, Good Good chief executive officer Matt Kendrick said they "remain committed to earning back" the tour's trust.

"We recognise that we have work to do as an organisation, and our focus right now is on our team, our culture and ensuring we learn from this situation." Kendrick added in a statement.

articles.title: Itauma vs Hrgovic: Can fast-tracked 21-year-old Briton make history on Saturday?
articles.text:
British heavyweight Moses Itauma pulls out his phone and scrolls through his pictures.

He shows a meme featuring former Nigerian president Olusegun Obasanjo in traditional attire, standing with his hands on his hips and staring deadpan into the camera.

"This is how an African dad looks at you when you pursue a career that goes against his wishes and you turn out to be successful," a chuckling Itauma reads aloud to BBC Sport. "That is pretty much my dad."

Itauma was born in Slovakia to a Nigerian father and a Slovak mother before moving to Kent as a young child.

His parents originally wanted him to become a doctor or a lawyer. But once his older brother turned professional and the family recognised Itauma's exceptional natural talent, their stance softened.

"Don't worry about school. Just focus on your boxing," his mother eventually said.

That decision has paid off spectacularly.

At 21, Itauma steps into the ring against Filip Hrgovic on Saturday for the vacant IBF title with the chance to become the second-youngest world heavyweight champion in history.

"There's a lot of expectations on my shoulders to carry the flag of British boxing. I just have to live up to it," Itauma says.

Victory against Croatia's Hrgovic would put Itauma on the path to becoming the next big name in British heavyweight boxing, with Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua inching closer to the end of their storied careers.

Fury, with his Netflix documentaries and larger-than-life personality, has always made himself the attraction. Itauma is more like Joshua - guarded and keeping the media at arm's length.

"What irritates me most is when people think you're public property," he says.

"What people don't know about me is that I don't actually want to be in the limelight. The way my career is going, I just have no choice."

Like Joshua, Itauma often appears uninterested in the theatrics of fight week. When Hrgovic interrupted during Thursday's news conference, Itauma calmly asked host Adam Smith for the next question.

There are similarities in their careers, too.

Joshua fought Charles Martin for the IBF title in his 16th pro bout, having boxed 34 rounds. Itauma arrives at his first world-title opportunity a fight sooner and with 31 rounds logged.

While Joshua had an Olympic gold medal and a deeper amateur background, victory for Itauma would make comparisons unavoidable - eclipsing Joshua to become the fastest British heavyweight to win a world title.

Itauma's trainer Ben Davison, who also worked with Joshua and Fury, believes he has the temperament to handle what comes next.

"Pressure is a privilege," he says.

"Moses has already had that pressure for such a long time and I just think it's water off a duck's back."

Boxing's best young prospects tend to be handled carefully and are given time to learn before dangerous tests arrive.

Itauma, however, has been fast-tracked to his world-title shot.

Francis Warren - son of Queensberry chief Frank - first noticed him as a teenager, sparring established professionals. Former British heavyweight champion Jeamie 'TKV' Tshikeva was there even earlier.

"Moses was a big 11 or 12-year-old, around 75 to 80kg, (11st 11lb to 12st 8lb) and sparred an adult of the same weight," TKV says. "He really showed up, put hands on this grown man, and I was shocked.

"The guy he sparred was around 25. Imagine going home and telling your wife you got beat up by a kid."

Itauma's progress has been marked by destructive stoppages over Dillian Whyte and Jermaine Franklin. They may not be world-beaters, but the manner of those wins strengthened belief Itauma was destined for the top.

When Oleksandr Usyk vacated the IBF title and Frank Sanchez agreed to step aside, Itauma's fight with Hrgovic was elevated into a world-title contest.

Suddenly, the fast track looked, to some, like a shortcut.

Hrgovic - even before the IBF belt was on the line - claimed Itauma had been handed "everything on a plate". On social media, there was a similar feeling - perhaps a final eliminator would have been a more natural way to earn his shot.

Itauma, though, has little interest in proving himself to the doubters.

"It's a lose-lose situation for me because if I win, I've done what people expect, and if I lose, it's just like, I wasn't as good as what I thought," he says.

"I don't find happiness in trying to please other people's expectations."

But what happens when his power does not end the fight? What happens when an opponent is still standing in round eight, still dangerous, still coming back?

TKV, who has sparred Joshua, Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley, has seen enough behind closed doors to believe Itauma can handle it.

"Moses works hard even though he hasn't had to face adversity in his fights or training," he says. "I've never seen him slack. He's fast, sharp, a good learner and I rarely see him get hit.

"I believe he can do the rounds, too. He has the potential to dominate the division for years."

There is no doubt within Itauma's camp that he belongs at this level. But all the outside questions over timing, merit and readiness will fade when the first bell sounds.

On Saturday, the prodigy has 12 rounds - if he needs them - to write his own chapter in heavyweight history.

articles.title: Sheffield artist defends "unfinished" Ronnie O'Sullivan mural
articles.text:
A Sheffield street artist has defended his mural of snooker player Ronnie O'Sullivan after the design received criticism - saying that the project is "unfinished".

Chris Ashmore was commissioned to produce the artwork featuring seven-time world champion O'Sullivan for the back wall of the Spot On Snooker Club on Langsett Road.

Although many residents said they liked the mural, others described it as "zombie-like", "shocking" and O'Sullivan's face as "skeletal".

Ashmore said he was surprised by the viral response online, but confirmed that he had only completed two weeks out of the five assigned to the job, and "touch-ups" were still needed.

The local artist said part of the problem was that he had been working from a scaffolding platform which obstructed his view, meaning he didn't get the "full perspective".

"I usually use a scissor lift, where you can stand back and see things as a whole, but I couldn't use it as the land is too uneven," he explained.

"When the scaffolding came down, I came away and boom - it's gone viral.

"I saw people saying it looks like Michael Jackson or a zombie. I've got thick skin, I'll be OK, but it didn't feel fair."

People living near the snooker and pool club had mixed feelings about the mural.

Gillian Jones said she liked it and it "brightened her day".

Glen Bridock said he was "a fan of the Rocket" and thought the design looked "brilliant".

Frank Short conceded that "the artwork is ok but the eyes are all wrong. It looks like he's taken something".

Shaun Spalding described the art as "shocking"

"His eyes are all wrong, his teeth are wrong, it just don't look like Ronnie. It looks like somebody who's got a skeletal face."

articles.title: Premier League predictions: Chris Sutton v Royal Blood drummer Ben Thatcher - & AI
articles.text:
Defending champions Arsenal made an impressive start to the season against newly promoted Coventry but face a tougher test against Aston Villa on Monday.

But with the number of outgoings at Villa Park, will it be another eye-opener for Unai Emery's men after last week's heavy defeat by Brighton?

BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton thinks so.

"There's only one winner with this," he said.

"Aston Villa had a slow start last season, they have lost big players and I just think Arsenal are going to run all over teams this season.

"I think they are going to get better and better which is ominous for everybody else."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week two, he takes on drummer Ben Thatcher from rock band Royal Blood.

Royal Blood's latest single, Ten Over Ten, is out now. It is taken from their fifth studio album, Dead Company, which is released in November.

Do you agree with their scores? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competitions.

Ben is a lifelong Brighton fan who is feeling optimistic about the new season despite seeing more star players like striker Danny Welbeck and defender Jan Paul van Hecke leave the club this summer.

"We loved Danny, because he really fitted into our style of play and he had such a great season last year," Ben told BBC Sport.

"We will miss Van Hecke at the back too, but the thing with Brighton is that we always bounce back. We always come through with the players we bring in that I've never heard of, but they get given this chance.

"I just trust in [Brighton owner] Tony Bloom. He knows better than anyone about these things, because he has done it so many times before.

"He has sold so many world-class players to other clubs and we have nurtured so many great players to replace them.

"So, I don't feel there is any need to worry right now. Just put the trust in the club and see how we get on.

"It's great to be back in Europe [in the Europa Conference League] but with us potentially playing so many more games, I don't expect us to get there again through our league position this time.

"But my hope is that we won't drop into the bottom half of the table. My thinking is that, as long as we finish in the top 10 again and have a good go at Europe, then that's a great season."

Chris Sutton and Ben Thatcher were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

Selhurst Park, 20:00 BST

Crystal Palace had a poor start away to Everton and it looks like there's a bit of interest from Liverpool in Ismaila Sarr.

The one thing they can't do before the end of the window is lose all the best players. But I do think they've got a goal in them.

I thought Man City deserved to win. They were a little bit clunky with Mark Guehi playing in midfield - a penny for the thoughts of Mateo Kovacic - but now they've got the youngster Ayyoub Bouaddi, although he'll need a bit of time to adapt.

I don't think this will be a cruise for City, I think they'll be pushed, but I think they'll get over the line. Erling Haaland didn't score last weekend so I expect him to get up to the mark.

Sutton's prediction: 1-3

Ben's prediction: Palace lost 3-0 to City home and away last season, but I reckon they will nab a goal this time. We are still waiting to see what City are like without Pep Guardiola which makes this harder to call. 1-3

AI's prediction: 1-3

I covered Nottingham Forest against Leeds last weekend and in fairness that was a really tight game. Oliver Glasner's gone into Forest with a big reputation but they went through four managers last year and the owner is notoriously impatient if things don't go well.

They didn't go big in the transfer window but they have got Liam Delap and he'll be hoping to get his career back on track. He had a disappointing season at Chelsea - which I know all about - but I do think there's a player in there and hopefully he'll he'll suit Forest.

It will be interesting to see who plays as that central striker. With the money they've spent on Delap then Chris Wood may not play a major role.

I thought Liverpool deserved a point at least at Newcastle and they got a fair bit of criticism but I can't see past the Liverpool win and I think Alexander Isak will get off the mark.

Last season he shot himself in the foot - forcing the move and then he had injury issues and it didn't quite happen for him. We know there's a player in there and for his sake and Liverpool's sake the sooner he comes to the fore the better.

Sutton's prediction: 2-1

Ben's prediction: This is a home win for Liverpool. 2-0

AI's prediction: 2-0

Vitality Stadium, 15:00

Bournemouth were resolute against Manchester City last week and they took the lead. The way in which they lost with the two late goals would have felt a real gut-wrencher for them.

Everton are off to a bit of a flyer under David Moyes - beating Palace and then Preston North End in the EFL Cup.

It will be interesting to see how Thierno Barry gets on because got a hat-trick against Preston in the Cup in midweek and I thought he was a bit of a nuisance last year to play against. He's still raw but I think he's got something.

I fancy Everton more than Bournemouth but I'm going to go for the draw.

Sutton's prediction: 1-1

Ben's prediction: Everton are going to nick this. 1-2

AI's prediction: 1-1

Coventry Building Society Arena, 15:00

I thought Andros Townsend was a bit harsh on Coventry on the Monday Night Club talking about the way they were beaten by Arsenal. I think Arsenal have the best team, the best squad and I don't think we can really judge Coventry on that.

Dean Holden - Hull's assistant manager - has talked about the way that Hull were going to play and then they go and back it up and beat Manchester United in the way that they did.

I think seven or eight of the team were playing in the Championship last season so this is a big game because you can imagine Coventry fans thinking this is a great chance at home to get three points after a tough start.

But Hull will go into this thinking if they can go back-to-back then what a start that is because they've been written off by idiots like myself. But I am going to edge Coventry at home.

Sutton's prediction: 2-0

Ben's prediction: This has worked out in my favour, having two promoted teams playing each other. It's going to be a cagey game because they will both want to get over each other, but I can see Coventry coming out on top. 1-0

AI's prediction: 2-1

Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, 17:30

We all thought this was going to be Tottenham's season but their defeat by Brentford was one of the extreme results at the weekend.

Roberto de Zerbi's said after the game that the players weren't fit enough, lost all the duels, weren't physical enough then used excuses about the pre-season and players coming in after the World Cup.

It looks like Newcastle are going to be the counter-attack kings this season. They've brought Nico Gonzalez in but whether he'll start I'm not sure but they have got pace as well.

Anthony Elanga scored last week having not scored at all in the Premier League last season but I have to say I haven't got a clue what this will be. I'm going to go for a Spurs win but I couldn't tell you why.

Sutton's prediction: 2-1

Ben's prediction: Spurs had a terrible season last time but they have had so many good players come in, while Newcastle have kind of done the opposite. Still, I am basing my prediction on Spurs boss Roberto de Zerbi because I watched him so many times at Brighton - and I am going for a draw. 2-2

AI's prediction: 1-2

Stamford Bridge, 14:00

Brighton are off to a flying start and it was a great opening result and performance by Xabi Alonso's Chelsea, winning the west London derby against Fulham.

Chelsea have got some talented players and, because they've got no European football, they're going to have a good crack in the Premier League this season.

What interested me against Fulham is Chelsea didn't have a lot of possession, but they were effective when they did have possession.

But Brighton are just one of those teams. I don't think I predicted a single Brighton result right last season they're just impossible to call.

I really like Jack Hinshelwood he's such an exciting young player and there's a good history with his family in football and connection to Brighton.

But I'm going to say Chelsea carry on this run and get the three points.

Sutton's prediction: 2-1

Ben's prediction: I have to go with my team. It is going to be close - well, actually I don't know if it will be close... but I have just got to go with it. 1-2

Ben on which Brighton players will shine this season: We have managed to hang on to Bart Verbruggen, which was massive, and we have still got Georginio Rutter, who scored an amazing goal in pre-season against Roma, and then there is also Yasin Ayari.

But I've heard some amazing things about our Greek players Charalampos Kostoulas and Stefanos Tzimas, who we did not see much of last season. They will be like new signings for us.

AI's prediction: 2-1

Elland Road, 14:00

Leeds and Daniel Farke proved loads of people wrong last season. But they were pretty cagey against Nottingham Forest last week in the Premier League.

They weren't very creative but then they got the job done against them in the EFL Cup in midweek and because of that I can't see Leeds losing.

Brentford are off to an absolute flyer - smashing Tottenham then hitting Birmingham for six or seven. They've started well with all the talk about their new midfielder Mamadou Sangare who now looks a bargain.

I think this is going to be really tight because Brentford like to play on the counter-attack.

Sutton's prediction: 1-1

Ben's prediction: This will definitely be close. 0-1

AI's prediction: 2-2

Old Trafford, 16:30

Well done to Ipswich for their start. It took them 11 games to get the first win under Kieran McKenna the last time they were in the Premier League and they've got off to a great start already.

Under Gary O'Neil they have got a bit about them - they've got players who can get them up the pitch, they have got pace with Daizen Maeda and Emersonn looks a bit of a handful.

I think they could cause United one or two problems but it's unthinkable that Manchester United could lose their opening two games of the season. Their start was an absolute stinker - they were very flat against Hull.

With respect, it was an open goal start for the season for them, with Hull then Ipswich - two promoted sides - and it would be bordering on catastrophic for Michael Carrick if they lose again.

I remember the days when United used to beat Ipswich 9-0 but I don't think it will be nine and I think Ipswich will score. I think Ipswich will score first but United will come from behind to win - panic over, Carrick's the king again.

Sutton's prediction: 2-1

Ben's prediction: As much as I'd like to say Ipswich will win this, they won't. 2-0

AI's prediction: 3-1

There's only one winner with this.

I'm a massive fan of Unai Emery but the Ollie Watkins thing sickens you a bit, he was really let down by his striker last week.

Aston Villa had a slow start last season, they have lost big players and I just think Arsenal are going to run all over teams this season.

Physically the will be too strong and they played some good stuff against Coventry. I think they are going to get better and better which is ominous for everybody else.

I wouldn't totally rule Emery and Villa out of it because you just don't know. They're very principled in the way they play, probably the most principled team in the Premier League in the way that they build from the back.

But I think Arsenal will swarm all over them.

Sutton's prediction: 0-2

Ben's prediction: Arsenal to take it, just about. 1-2

AI's prediction: 1-3

articles.title: US Open 2026: Why does Venus Williams get so many wildcards?
articles.text:
Venus Williams has broken many acres of new ground as a tennis player, with five Wimbledon singles titles among her multiple achievements.

The 46-year-old has been playing professionally for nearly 30 years, but her last 14 singles matches have all ended in defeat.

With a world ranking of 611, Williams is reliant on wildcards to compete.

She has had 11 already this season - and the United States Tennis Association (USTA) has offered her a 12th so she can play at the US Open, where she will face fellow Grand Slam champion Sofia Kenin in the first round.

There is a school of thought that argues that, without any wins, it is simply too many, irrespective of her previous achievements.

But there is no limit to the number of wildcards a Grand Slam champion can receive and, for many tournaments, having a Williams sister on site still makes commercial sense.

"I think it's good for tennis to have these generational icons," said Karl Hale, the tournament director who offered Williams a wildcard for this month's WTA 1000 event in Toronto.

"That they are still allocating wildcards for them says something to their intrinsic value to the tournaments."

Two-time US Open singles champion Williams has not qualified for a Grand Slam by ranking since Wimbledon 2021, which is also where she recorded her most recent singles win at a major.

She has been competitive in her past two Slam singles matches, pushing 11th seed Karolina Muchova to three sets in New York last year, and narrowly losing in three sets to Olga Danilovic at January's Australian Open.

Williams was also a doubles quarter-finalist at last year's US Open, but the defeat by qualifier Emiliana Arango in Cincinnati this month was her 18th loss in 19 singles matches. The only bright spot has been a win over Peyton Stearns in Washington last July.

And yet this year alone tournament directors in New Zealand, Australia, Spain, Germany and Canada - as well as the United States - have wanted Williams at their events.

Eight of the 128 spots in a Grand Slam singles draw are assigned to wildcards, and usually between four and eight at WTA and ATP events depending on the size of the field.

"The way we looked at Venus is that her legacy is phenomenal," Hale told BBC Sport.

"She's done so much for the sport and is really popular here in Toronto and our markets specifically - so we thought it was really good to announce it early that we have a Williams sister coming."

Hale says the media interest was significant, which he believes in turn drives ticket sales.

"The wildcards always play first-round matches, and with the bigger draw [size] now, it adds more notable names and stars for the beginning of the tournament," he said.

"Venus played opening day. She kicked off our tournament, so it added a lot of value."

Most tournaments will prioritise their own national players for wildcards, but they are also given to names who are likely to add commercial value to the event.

There are also what Hale calls 'trades' with other national federations or agencies like IMG, which manages players and until recently also owned the Miami and Madrid Opens.

The most obvious example of a 'trade' is the reciprocal wildcard agreement between the USTA, Tennis Australia and the French Tennis Federation. Each of these Grand Slam nations offers a men's and a women's wildcard to the others, knowing two of their players will benefit when it is their counterparts' turn to host.

One sporting event which has reduced the opportunity for past champions to return is the Open Golf Championship.

Twenty years ago, any champions under 65 could play whenever they wished. Now, winners only get the chance to return until they are 55, which could open up the odd place in the field to younger, more highly ranked professionals.

Golfers can be competitive for much longer, but there are no limits in tennis. Martina Navratilova was given a wildcard for both the 2004 French Open and Wimbledon - and won a round on the grass - when she made a comeback aged 47.

"You never want to put a player out there that you are unsure about," said Hale, who believes Williams is still capable of winning matches.

"Venus lost 6-4 6-1 to Kamilla Rakhimova, and the first set was really competitive. She's still competitive, but just not winning these matches."

So should there be a limit; a moment when a tournament director offers the spot to a more highly ranked player trying to advance their career?

"When the time comes that Venus is not competitive in sets, then I think she will make that call," Hale responded.

"Venus and Serena have done so much for women's tennis and the sport that they should be able to play as long as they want.

"I'm very happy they are continuing and they make their decision when they are ready, or each tournament makes their decision when they are ready."

British number one Katie Boulter put it a similar way after she partnered the "absolute icon" in the Madrid doubles in April.

"Venus has given so much to our sport that she deserves to get what she needs back," she said then.

"We have to be grateful that she is still out there, doing the best she can."

articles.title: Asia Games: Hosts say no room for extra competitors
articles.text:
The hosts of next month's Asian Games in Japan have told athletes to "make their own arrangements" for accommodation after running out of rooms for them.

Initially, 15,000 athletes and officials were expected to attend the Games, which will be held in the Nagoya and Aichi region between 19 September and 4 October.

However, last week the Olympic Council of Asia confirmed the number would be closer to 17,000 after teqball - which combines elements of football and table tennis - and padel were included earlier this year.

The mayor of Nagoya and acting chairman of the local organising committee, Ichiro Hirosawa, said it was "difficult to accommodate this number" because the Games is "operating on a tight budget".

Hideaki Omura, president of the organising committee and Governor of Aichi Prefecture, said the hosts have "neither the manpower nor the budget to make the necessary arrangements" for the late influx of athletes.

"The host city agreement specifies a delegation of 15,000 people," explained Omura. "We have not set aside a budget for any more than that.

"There is simply nowhere for them to stay. If they still wish to come, they will have to make their own arrangements."

Unlike the Olympic Games, where there is a designated athletes' village, organisers have opted to use temporary accommodation for competitors.

Between 4,000 and 5,000 athletes will stay on board the Italian cruise ship Costa Serena that will be docked in the area, while a further 2,000 will use shipping container-style huts.

The remaining athletes and officials will be accommodated in hotels in Tokyo, where swimming, diving and equestrian events are scheduled to take place.

articles.title: Women's Super League: Brighton boss Dario Vidosic leaves club
articles.text:
Brighton manager Dario Vidosic is leaving the Women's Super League club just a week before the start of the season "to pursue a new opportunity".

It is a major blow for Brighton, who reached the Women's FA Cup final for the first time in the club's history in May under Vidosic.

The Australian joined from Melbourne City in 2024 and signed a three-year deal as Brighton sought to close in on the WSL's top four.

In his first season in charge, Vidosic led them to a fifth-placed finish - their best in the WSL - and they recorded memorable wins over Arsenal and Manchester City in 2025-26.

"I have loved my time at Albion and am proud of what we have achieved together," Vidosic said.

"Leaving has been a difficult decision but I believe it is the right time for me and my family to begin a new chapter.

"I would like to thank the players, staff and supporters for their support throughout my time at the club and wish everyone associated with Albion every success."

With a week to go before the new season, Brighton were being tipped as one of the club's capable of challenging WSL big hitters Arsenal, Chelsea, Manchester City and Manchester United for a top-four place.

Reports in Spain, external suggest Arturo Ruiz - who has just left Real Sociedad - is lined up to be Vidosic's replacement at Brighton.

Sources say Vidosic could be heading to the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) in the United States, with Angel City the most likely destination.

Brighton kick off their WSL season at home to Arsenal on Sunday, 6 September (12:00 BST).

articles.title: Diamond League results: Audrey Werro comes up just short in 800m world record bid
articles.text:
European champion Audrey Werro came tantalisingly close to downing the oldest outdoor world record in athletics, finishing a little more than four tenths of a second off Jarmila Kratochvilova's 800m mark of one minute 53.28 seconds, set 43 years ago.

Roared on by a 25,000-strong capacity crowd at the Zurich Diamond League, the Swiss hit the final 100m almost in stride with the infield pacing lights which had been set for a world record.

However Werro, straining hard against the clock, could not quite find the finishing pace she needed, clocking 1:53.70.

Still, the third-fastest time in history shaves another tenth of a second off the 22-year-old's personal best and only increases the sense that she will break the record sooner rather than later.

"As far as the world record is concerned, I saw the light, but there was a lot of movement during the race and it was not calm," said Werro, who caused second-placed Femke Broeders-Bol to check as she overtook the Dutchwoman at the start of her kick for home on the back straight.

"I still had enough energy at the end of the race to accelerate and to stay in the lead. Yes, it was tight for the world record, it was not meant for today.

"I am so proud to be able to run those sub-1:54 times, which shows that I can run consistently and fast now and this is good for the future."

Werro has improved every year of her top-level career and now, having finished her studies and concentrating on the track, has shown ruthless consistency. She has four of the top-10 all-time 800m times, all clocked this summer.

For Britain's Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson, who withdrew from the meeting after her exertions in taking continental silver behind Werro in Birmingham, it only emphasised the challenge she faces in the event.

Not only does she have to contend with Werro's burgeoning form, but Broeders-Bol, the world 400m hurdles champion who has switched up to two laps this season, gave another impressive showing in her debut campaign over 800m.

The Dutchwoman, who took out the pace initially, clocked a new national record of 1:54.71, beating Hodgkinson's training partner and Commonwealth 800m champion Georgia Hunter-Bell, who finished in 1:55.03, into third.

Broeders-Bol's long, languid stride and sprint speed have already made an impression in the event and she is gaining tactical knowhow fast as she acclimatises to the bump and hustle of middle distance.

"I was hoping to be in these sort of fights, but to be honest, I didn't expect it at all in the first season," she said afterwards.

"I thought I needed at least one or two seasons to get into the 1:54s, but here I am."

When Athing Mu-Nikolayev, Hodgkinson's American nemesis who beat her to gold at the Tokyo Olympics and Eugene 2022, slipped off the scene, the Briton had hoped to dominate the 800m.

With less than two years until she defends her Olympic crown in Los Angeles however, new rivals are looking ever more threatening.

Hodgkinson, like Werro and Broeders-Bol, has qualified for the Diamond League final in Brussels on 4-5 September. It could be an intriguing benchmark for the season's end.

While Werro fell short in her world record attempt, two new marks were set in an astonishng night of action.

Amy Hunt, winner of four golds at the European Championships earlier this month, found things tougher against some of the world's finest 100m runners.

Left in the blocks, the Briton had to watch on as Olympic champion Julien Alfred inflicted Melissa Jefferson-Wooden's first defeat over the distance in two years, edging out the American in a 10.70-second photo finish.

David Rudisha's 800m world record of one minute 40.91 seconds, set en route to gold at London 2012, survived unscathed as his Kenyan compatriot Emmanuel Wanyonyi came home in one minute 41.76 seconds.

While Sweden's Armand 'Mondo' Duplantis, pushed on by competition from Greece's Emmanouil Karalis, failed in three shots at improving his own pole vault world record to 6.32m.

Jakob Ingebrigtsen, who has been booked in for a keenly-anticipated duel with Britain's Josh Kerr at the inaugural Ultimate Championships on 11-13 September, could only finish fifth in a 1500m race won by American Olympic champion Cole Hocker.

articles.title: Premier League: How top-flight officials adapt to pace of games
articles.text:
Referees know every decision will be scrutinised.

Fans, pundits and players will pour over their calls, creating never-ending debates.

It is why they are prepared.

Many of the Professional Referee Group, the top officials in the country, have met in Loughborough this week.

They meet every few weeks to work and train together, with the officials spread across the country.

Lunch is a choice of chicken, teriyaki beef or tofu with vegetables and salad, with protein bars and rice cakes alongside the fruit, granola and Greek yogurts.

It is a reminder of the environment. Since becoming professional in 2001 top flight officials have had to adapt.

"I never thought referees did as much as what we do now," says Sam Allison, who played for Chippenham Town and Frome Town during his playing career, which started at Swindon.

"We are training full-time, sometimes two, three sessions a day, making sure that we are ready on a Saturday afternoon.

"Some of it (not understanding referees' workload) is probably ignorance, lack of awareness, lack of communication being disseminated to people out there.

"I think of my ignorance of just thinking referees just turned up, refereed the game and then went home.

"We have all the preparation, all the training, all the sacrifices, all the commitment, all the desire, all the support networks, people investing in you to make sure that you are ready in the best position to deliver a game."

Allison, a former firefighter, is the fourth official for Manchester City's trip to Crystal Palace on Friday while colleague Sam Barrott has been given Saturday's early match between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest.

Barrott took charge of Arsenal's Community Shield win over Manchester City this month and was in the Faroe Islands on 20 August to referee Ki Klaksvik's 0-0 draw with Riga in the Europa Conference League.

Different teams and different tactics means a different approach to each game, with officials prepping with Pro Ref's analysis team who provide key information to understand the way a team is going to play, to support the flow of the game.

It comes after a summer of work to ensure the officials can match - and better - the demands of the Premier League.

"At the moment we've got five substitutions and we see all the time fresh legs for teams can change the momentum in a game," said Barrott.

"If three new attacking players are on that are all very pacey after 70 minutes you know they're going to change the way they play, they're going to try and push.

"That normally means an increase in output for us and when that happens, there's not a point in us where we go, we can't handle this'.

"We've been trying to push the demands of where we are, everybody's trying to get better. Football has the 1% gains, every game or every training session we're very similar in the mindset, we want to be better."

Francis Bunce has been with Pro Ref - rebranded from the Professional Game Match Officials Limited - for 10 years and is now the physical performance manager.

He was with the group in Spain last month for their pre-season training camp, putting them through what is viewed as the infamous Maximal Aerobic Speed (MAS) test - an all out six-minute run.

"When you look at refereeing in the Premier League and Championship people very rarely talk about their physical qualities or physical capabilities," he tells BBC Sport.

"They've all done so well to keep developing and they look like athletes on the pitch - they are athletes.

"We're in a very different space with match officials, they are naturally some years older than the players and you can't get away from that because having a 21-year-old referee would be very difficult in the Premier League with everything you need to learn and experience.

"They should be definitely considered as athletes and if you then compare them to Joe Public who might want to shout some views from the sidelines, they wouldn't be able to keep up for a minute with what some of our guys can do."

With officials training remotely for part of the week, they need to be monitored with heart rate and GPS technology.

All the officials are on tailored plans and work in a group of around five once or twice a week at local hubs where strength and conditioning sessions are delivered.

Those at the World Cup - referees Michael Oliver and Anthony Taylor, along with assistants Gary Beswick, Adam Nunn, Stuart Burt and James Mainwaring - also had special training this summer, running and cycling in chambers of around 40 degrees to prepare them for the intense heat at the tournament.

Last season referees ran a total of 3.6m metres, with their overall sprint distance 12,136m.

At the weekend, Stuart Attwell covered the fourth highest distance of anyone on the pitch while taking charge of Newcastle's 2-2 draw with Liverpool, awarding the Reds a stoppage time penalty.

He was also fifth for highest high-speed running, therefore beating all but four players.

"A lot of people could go and run around the pitch but they wouldn't be able to pick up those key positions to make those defining decisions," says Bunce.

"That's something that's really important we build into our training, in terms of how we improve speed, how we improve being able to physically exert that kind of acceleration or high-speed running into a game.

"Then make a decision and to do it in a cool, calm manner and potentially have to make a VAR announcement and sound completely like they haven't been running around for 90 minutes."

The work pays off with Barrott recalling an incident in a match between Brighton and Fulham which underlined why it is worth it.

It came in March 2025 when he awarded a late penalty after Harrison Reed fouled Joao Pedro and the striker scored the injury-time penalty to earn the Seagulls a 2-1 win.

"I'm stood at the edge of the box, everyone turns and you're pointing at the penalty spot. There wasn't anything in me that thought 'you've got that wrong'," says Barrott.

"It was complete confidence, all because I'm stood in the right spot and to do that. It involves a little bit of football knowledge, anticipating what could happen and what we would call a danger area.

"But then also knowing what you've done for weeks and weeks - and potentially years and years - has allowed you to move into that position without having to think.

"It's just subconscious, it just happens and you're not stood there thinking: 'I'm tired, do I need to make that run?'

"That never comes into the thought process anymore, and the fatigue aspect of it never crosses your mind because we are where we need to be."

articles.title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America
articles.text:
US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.

The move comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed last week, and the US imposed new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter tariffs next month.

Trump said the move to rename the lake, which straddles both countries, was effective immediately. He has broad discretion over how the US recognises landmarks but other countries do not have to follow.

In response, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said "things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever".

Text of the executive order says it gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US.

Carney noted that the name Lake Ontario could be traced back more than 400 years, adding that it preceded the formation of the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

"We know that the United States is changing. Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms.

"Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever."

There is no universally recognised international body setting the names of international waters.

When Trump took to the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.

It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application., external

In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)".

The White House at the time also blocked Associated Press reporters from presidential events over the news agency's refusal to adopt the name "Gulf of America" in its coverage. The AP sued the Trump administration in response, and that legal battle is ongoing.
